content.text: {"relation":"MATCH","consensus_summary":"The tares symbolize the 'sons/children of the evil one' — counterfeit or false persons (often applied as false believers) sown by the devil among the true children of the kingdom, indistinguishable until maturity, left to coexist until the end-of-age harvest when angels separate and burn them. This is unusually settled because Jesus supplies the interpretation in Matthew 13:36-43; residual debate concerns only whether the field is the world or the church and what applications follow.","book_summary":"The tares are the counterfeit sown among the wheat by the enemy — a weed mimicking true grain until harvest, then bound and burned; identified as the children of the wicked one, and noted as distinct from winnowed chaff.","consensus_core_identification":"Tares = the children/sons of the evil one, counterfeit persons sown by the devil among the righteous, coexisting until final judgment separation.","book_core_identification":"Tares = the children of the wicked one, the enemy-sown counterfeit that mimics wheat until harvest, then is gathered and burned.","core_relation":"EQUIVALENT","extension_relation":"SAME_CASES","boundary_disagreement":"None of substance. The book's added note that tares are 'distinct from the winnowed chaff' is a taxonomic clarification distinguishing this symbol from a different image (Matt 3:12), not a change to which persons or cases the tares cover. Response A even cites the chaff imagery as a parallel, but treating it as a parallel versus a distinct symbol does not alter the identification of the tares themselves.","material_contradiction":"None. Both readings identify the tares as the devil-sown children of the wicked one, counterfeits among the true, destined for burning at the end-time harvest.","rationale":"The book's entry reproduces the consensus core almost verbatim from Matthew 13:38 ('the tares are the children of the wicked one') and preserves every structural element the consensus emphasizes: enemy sowing (the devil), mimicry of true grain (the counterfeit theme all four responses highlight via darnel's resemblance to wheat), coexistence until harvest, and binding/burning at judgment. The only distinctive touch — distinguishing tares from chaff — is a precision about adjacent symbols rather than a refinement of the tares' extension or conditions. No boundary, condition, or referent is changed, so this is a MATCH rather than REFINED.","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"One could argue the book's explicit demarcation from chaff, and its emphasis on 'counterfeit' mimicry, slightly sharpens the referent toward false professors specifically (versus the wicked generally), which might suggest REFINED. But the consensus responses already include the counterfeit/false-believer framing as the primary meaning, and the chaff distinction concerns a different symbol, not the tares' extension, so the objection does not overturn MATCH.","confidence":"high"}
